title: *S&PGRBulletin: CHF Loan Law A Remote Risk For Slovenian Banks
text:
2 Feb 2022 12:44 ET  Press Release: S&PGRBulletin: CHF Loan Law A Remote Risk For Slovenian Banks


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
FRANKFURT (S&P Global Ratings) Feb. 2, 2022--S&P Global Ratings said today 
said that the Slovenian parliament's vote to introduce a law requiring banks 
to compensate loan holders for exchange-rate losses on Swiss franc (CHF) loans 
poses a remote risk to the Slovenian banking sector. Consequently, we do not 
see the law as having a direct immediate bearing on our banking industry 
country risk assessment for Slovenia. 
 
The law retroactively introduces a cap on the exchange rate on retail loans 
issued between 2004 and 2010 and denominated in Swiss francs, or denominated 
in the domestic currency, but with the amount of interest or principal linked 
to the Swiss franc. The cap would be activated when a change in the 
euro-to-Swiss franc exchange rate caused the credit balance or repayment 
installments to differ by more than 10% compared to the exchange rate when the 
loan was drawn down. The law largely concerns long-term mortgages, regardless 
of any violations of the requirement to inform clients of certain risks when 
they took out the loans, or of whether the loans have been fully repaid, 
terminated, or sold to third parties. 
 
We understand that the retroactive application of the law could contradict 
Slovenian and the European legislation, making the implementation of the law 
highly doubtful. The Bank of Slovenia  and the European Central Bank  have 
claimed that the law violates both Slovenian and EU  law, and we expect that 
Slovenian banks will challenge the law in the constitutional court on these 
grounds. We note, however, that there is a general election scheduled for 
April this year in Slovenia. This may affect the legislative process, and thus 
adds uncertainty to the outcome. 
 
The banks have estimated that, if enacted, the law would cause a EUR300 
million loss. This would materially strain their profitability in the year the 
law was enacted, but we believe that the effect would remain manageable thanks 
to the banks' solid capital buffers and operating performance. Slovenian banks 
recorded sector-wide net profits of EUR473 million in the year to November 
2021. Additionally, about 65% of domestic banking assets belong to banks that 
are part of larger foreign groups, which, in our view, would provide a second 
line of defense if necessary. However, we acknowledge that the estimate of 
loss is highly uncertain, and that it depends, among other things, on the 
evolution of the euro-to-Swiss franc exchange rate. Moreover, the banks will 
likely be affected to varying degrees. At the same time, the share of Swiss 
franc-linked loans in the private sector is less than 2% of total loans, and, 
as such, adverse movements in exchange rates would be unlikely to increase 
credit losses materially. 
 
If losses occur, we view the estimated amount as unlikely to destabilize the 
Slovenian banking industry. However, the adoption of the law on a retroactive 
basis could bring into question the predictability of Slovenia's legal 
framework and increase uncertainty about negative intervention by the future 
government in the banking sector. As a result, if we thought that the 
likelihood of the law being enacted was increasing, we could consider revising 
our view of industry risk in Slovenia's banking industry to a weaker 
assessment. We could take a similar action if the discussions around the 
introduction of the law turned out to be the starting point for a series of 
unfavorable laws for the domestic banking sector. We will also monitor 
potential negative shifts in foreign investor sentiment, as these could 
increase economic risks in the country. 
 
This report does not constitute a rating action.

title: *S&PGR Revises Slovenia Outlook To Pos; Affirms 'A/A-1' Ratings
text:
16 Dec 2016 11:36 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Slovenia Outlook To Pos; Affirms 'A/A-1' Ratings


 
 
The following is a press release from Standard & Poor's: 
OVERVIEW 
 
     -- We project Slovenia's robust economic growth will persist in 2017-2019. 
     -- Monetary conditions are gradually normalizing and non-performing 
exposures have reduced sizably, and, despite the current budgetary pressures, 
we expect Slovenia's government debt relative to GDP to continue on a downward 
path over 2017-2019. 
     -- As a result, we are revising our outlook on Slovenia to positive from 
stable, and affirming our 'A/A-1' long- and short-term sovereign credit 
ratings. 
     -- The positive outlook reflects our view of at least a one-in-three 
likelihood that we will raise our ratings on Slovenia over the next two years 
if we observe further improvements in the country's transmission of monetary 
policy and budgetary position, with a decline in general government debt. 
 
RATING ACTION 
 
On Dec. 16, 2016, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on the Republic of 
Slovenia to positive. At the same time, we affirmed our 'A/A-1' long- and 
short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Slovenia. 
 
RATIONALE 
 
The outlook revision reflects our expectation that the recovery of the 
Slovenian economy will continue at a solid pace. We now estimate that the 
Slovenian economy will grow by about 2.5% in 2016 and accelerate to 2.7% in 
2017, supported by strong net exports and increasing private consumption. The 
latter will be supported by higher disposable incomes thanks to improving labor 
market conditions, low, albeit slowly increasing, inflation and likely public 
sector wage hikes, as well as growing household credit. In addition to domestic 
demand, Slovenia's economy will continue to be supported by the country's 
competitive export-oriented economic structure. Private investment will further 
underpin export potential, for example as production in the automotive sector 
is extended. In that regard, we expect manufacturing to remain an important 
sector for Slovenian economic growth over the projection horizon. As the output 
gap narrows and wages continue to increase, we anticipate that inflation will 
be over 1% in 2017. 
 
We also believe that the implementation of growth-enhancing structural reforms, 
including in judicial and administrative areas, could further boost Slovenia's 
medium-to-long-term economic growth prospects, while health care system reform 
could improve prospects for government finances over time. Furthermore, the 
educational system plays an increasingly important role in preserving the 
international competitiveness that the open Slovenian economy enjoys. Although 
the economy benefits from its openness to international trade (exports of goods 
and services will amount to about 80% of GDP this year), in our view, 
significant administrative barriers, e.g., in judiciary, still inhibit business 
and investments. 
 
The continuing deepening of international linkages will remain positive for the 
Slovenian economy and, with strengthening trade and services balances, we 
expect the current account to remain in surplus of over 6% of GDP on average 
over 2016-2019 despite rising imports as investment and consumption increase. 
While the external deleveraging of the financial sector continues, firms have 
increasingly relied on alternatives to bank funding to finance investments, for 
example own reserves, intercompany loans, or foreign debt issuance. Despite the 
pickup in consumer credit in recent months, we believe credit growth will 
likely remain subdued in 2017. While we still view the monetary and credit 
transmission mechanism to the real economy in Slovenia as hampered due to the 
recent banking crisis, despite the European Central Bank's (ECB's) expansionary 
monetary stance, we expect banking sector activities and monetary conditions to 
continue to normalize in 2017. In that vein, we anticipate that the ratio of 
nonperforming loans of 6.4% (as of September 2016) will further decline, given 
the economic growth and further restructuring efforts, especially in the small 
and midsize enterprises sector. We also note that, following years of 
deleveraging, the corporate debt-to-GDP ratio has reduced to below the euro 
area average. 
 
We believe that rising domestic demand and the recent strong labor market 
performance--with the unemployment rate decreasing from around 8% on average in 
2016 to 7.7% at year-end 2017--will support the authorities' budgetary 
consolidation efforts. We project the general government deficit to average 
1.8% of GDP over 2016-2019, with the deficit in 2017 likely slightly higher 
than envisaged by the government, depending on the outcome of ongoing 
negotiations on public sector wages and the stance on relieving consolidation 
measures introduced in past years. We also expect government investment to 
resume following the break in 2015-2016 owing to the start of the new EU budget 
cycle. We nonetheless expect that the government will continue to focus on 
further narrowing the fiscal deficit and reducing the general government 
debt-to-GDP ratio. To this end, lawmakers have adopted a fiscal rule act that 
establishes limits for general government expenditures so as to achieve a 
structurally balanced budget in the medium term. 
 
We expect that, besides successively lower budget deficits, the drawdown of the 
government's existing cash buffer will drive the decrease in general government 
debt in nominal terms by 0.2% of GDP on average per year over 2016-2019. In our 
view, this will support a reduction in the gross general government debt as a 
share of GDP to about 69% in 2019 from 81% in 2015. 
 
At the same time, we project that the decline in the net government debt-to-GDP 
ratio will be around 2% of GDP over the same period. As with our treatment of 
the debt of all asset management companies ("bad banks"), our estimates of 
Slovenia's gross and net general government debt include obligations related to 
the Bank Asset Management Company (BAMC), issued to purchase loans and other 
distressed assets from participating Slovenian banks at a discount to market 
value. At the same time, we exclude from the general government debt stock the 
guarantees related to the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF; see "S&P 
Clarifies Its Approach To Accounting For EFSF Liabilities When Rating The 
Sovereign Guarantors," published Nov. 2, 2011, on RatingsDirect). We forecast 
the ratio of general government interest expenditures to general government 
revenues will be about 6% in 2016, down from 6.5% in 2015, before declining 
further thanks to the ECB's Public Sector Purchase Programme, which is 
currently scheduled to run until the end of 2017. 
 
In our forecast we do not incorporate any future proceeds from the ongoing 
privatization process (for example, of the largest state-owned bank Nova 
Ljubljanska Banka) or sale of assets from the BAMC, which took over 
nonperforming claims totaling EUR5 billion (about 12% of 2016 GDP) from the 
banking sector. If these sale revenues were applied to government debt 
reduction, net general government debt relative to GDP could decline at a 
faster pace than we currently anticipate. 
 
Following a protracted banking crisis, Slovenia's banking sector returned to 
profitability in 2015 and appears well capitalized. According to Bank of 
Slovenia data, the average capital adequacy ratio (on a solo basis) was 21.4% 
in September 2016, up by 0.5 percentage points compared with year-end 2015. We 
believe that the regulatory framework has materially strengthened, driven by 
the transfer of the supervisory functions to the ECB for the largest part of 
the banking system and a successful transition of local regulatory oversight. 
Market confidence in local banks remains weak, though, in our view, as they 
still have to demonstrate success and sustainability under the new setup after 
the recent years' restructuring. The repayment of substantial external 
liabilities and loan deleveraging, together with growth of customer deposits, 
has led to improvements in banks' funding positions, which we expect to 
persist. 
 
Although we consider that policy risks in Slovenia have receded since 2013 and 
the current government has survived several no-confidence votes, we cannot rule 
out disagreements among the government coalition parties along ideological 
lines, e.g., on the pace of the abovementioned reforms or on the role of the 
very large state-owned or -controlled enterprises in the economy, which could 
lead to early elections. We think that long-entrenched political patronage and 
only slowly improving institutional and corporate governance could hamper the 
pace and effectiveness of the abovementioned reforms, due to the vested 
interests of incumbents in these sectors. This could potentially slow the 
economic restructuring under way and prevent a more efficient allocation of 
resources in the economy, with negative implications for future economic growth 
prospects. In this context, we would view negatively any potential legislative 
efforts or government intervention aimed at weakening the independence of Bank 
of Slovenia, the country's central bank. 
 
OUTLOOK 
 
The positive outlook reflects our view that there is at least a one-in-three 
probability of an upgrade over the next two years if, alongside the continued 
economic recovery, we observe further improvements in the transmission of 
monetary policy to the real economy and budgetary position, with a decline in 
general government debt. 
 
We could revise the outlook to stable if we consider there is a risk of a 
material slippage in Slovenia's budgetary trajectory and a reversal in net 
general government debt dynamics, or if the current account turns into a 
deficit position, including for example due to a significantly weakened 
external macroeconomic environment. A weakening of Slovenia's key institutions 
or policy consensus across the currently governing coalition with the potential 
to hamper policy cohesiveness could also lead us to revise the outlook to 
stable.

title: *Fitch Affirms Slovenia at 'BBB+'; Outlook Stable
text:
27 Mar 2015 17:12 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Slovenia at 'BBB+'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings: 
 

Fitch Ratings-London/Hong Kong-27 March 2015: Fitch Ratings has affirmed Slovenia's Long-term foreign and local currency Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) at 'BBB+'. The Outlooks on the Long-term IDRs are Stable. The issue ratings on Slovenia's senior unsecured foreign and local currency bonds are also affirmed at 'BBB+'. The Country Ceiling is affirmed at 'AA+' and the Short-term foreign currency IDR at 'F2'.

KEY RATING DRIVERS

Slovenia's 'BBB+' IDRs and Stable Outlook reflect the following key rating drivers:

-Previous government interventions have reduced the sovereign's vulnerability to the banking sector. The aggregated Tier 1 capital ratio was 15.9% in September 2014, up from 10.2% at end-2012. Transfers of impaired assets to the Bad Asset Management Company (BAMC) have led to a decline in non-performing loans (over 90 days past due) to 11.6% in January 2015 from 18.1% in November 2013. The health of the banking sector remains fragile but Fitch believes the risks posed by the financial sector to government finances and the economy have reduced significantly.

-In 2015, Fitch expects the fiscal deficit will be 3% of GDP, smaller than 5.3% in 2014, due to expenditure restraint and efficiency gains on tax revenues. Crucially Fitch assumes that there will be no new budget support for banks in 2015 (after it cost the budget 9.5% of GDP in 2013 and 1.9% in 2014). The set-up of the bank resolution fund (totalling EUR350m and financed by banks) should help protect the budget from potential bank support.

-General government gross debt (82% of GDP in 2014) is much higher than the peers' median (41%), partly as a result of substantial interventions to support the banking sector. Debt is set to peak in 2015, at 83% of GDP, before declining, consistent with a tightening fiscal policy, real GDP growth of 2% and a recovery in inflation towards the 2% target. Debt reduction could benefit from a lower cash balance (government deposits are high, at 11.6% of GDP at end-2014) and the allocation of 90% of the proceeds from future privatisations.

-Five-year average GDP growth of 0.2% p.a. is much weaker than the 'BBB' range median of 3% or the 'A' range median of 3.2%, partly reflecting Slovenia's recent banking crisis. Unemployment, at 9.7% in 2014 (annual average), is also high versus peers. However, GDP grew 2.6% in 2014, after contracting 1% in 2013. The rebound was primarily driven by high exports (+6.3%) and investment (+3.6%), supported by exceptionally high European Union fund disbursement.

Fitch expects growth to remain around 2% in the medium term, supported by a gradual improvement in the external environment and in domestic demand, in line with the clean-up in banks and corporates' balance sheets.

-The combination of high current account surpluses and private external debt deleveraging is strengthening external metrics from a weak position. Fitch expects the current account surplus to have been 5.9% of GDP in 2014, supported by improved cost competitiveness, and to remain around 5% in the medium-term. Net external debt, at 35.4% of GDP in 2014, is still high relative to the 'BBB' median (7.9% of GDP) but down markedly from 42.4% in 2012. Fitch expects it will reach 18.7% of GDP by 2016.

-Income per head in purchasing power parity, indicators of human development and governance are much higher than the 'BBB' peers' median, reflecting Slovenia's fairly high value-added economy and membership to the European Union.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

The main factors that could lead to a positive rating action are:

-Budget deficit reduction consistent with government debt on a firm downward path

-Progress in the clean-up of bank and corporate balance sheets

-Sustained economic recovery supported by structural reforms

The main factors that could lead to a negative rating action are:

-Deterioration in government debt metrics

-Sustained macroeconomic underperformance and/or deterioration of financing conditions relative to Fitch's expectations

KEY ASSUMPTIONS

- Given the uncertainties involved, Fitch does not assume a contribution from the realisation of returns on distressed assets held on BAMC's balance sheet for its government debt projections. Likewise, Fitch does not take into account potential debt reduction from privatisation proceeds.

The European Central Bank's asset purchase programme should help underpin inflation expectations and support our base case that, in the context of a modest economic recovery, the eurozone will avoid prolonged deflation.

title: Central Bank  Boss Welcomes Fiscal Union Deal
text:
Ljubljana, 13 December (STA) - Marko Kranjec, the governor of Slovenia's

central bank, has labelled the recent EU agreement on a tighter fiscal

union a "good achievement of politicians in Brussels". This is the most

that could be expected, he told TV Slovenija late on Monday.

Kranjec said "radical changes" had been achieved with regard to the

harmonisation of public finances. "We are in a process of harmonisation

that has been difficult to imagine so far."

He is not surprised that rating agencies are less pleased with the deal,

but said he would not make too much out of it. As for capital markets, it

is still too early to make any conclusions.

Kranjec is convinced capital markets will "realise that this deal from

Brussels will be an important contribution to stabilisation and prevention

of the eurozone crisis."

The euro will persevere and Slovenia needs to keep it as its currency, he

said, noting that it would be bad for any country to abandon the euro and

revert back to its own currency.

With public finances looking increasingly shaky, some economists and

pundits have been warning that Slovenia will eventually have to accept some

sort of intervention from the EU or the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

But Kranjec labelled that notion an "excessive projection of our future

situation," arguing that politicians will find enough wisdom to take

appropriate measures on public finances, he said.

"It is not impossible to reduce the structural deficit to the required

level," he said. But he explained that the price for that will be lower GDP

growth, which will be the case for the entire EU.

title: Austria wants Slovenia to join euro in 2007-sources
text:
VIENNA, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Austria will lobby European Union finance ministers next week to allow Slovenia to adopt the euro currency in 2007, making it the first EU newcomer to join the euro, Austrian Finance Ministry sources said on Friday.  

The Baltic countries of Estonia and Lithuania, which along with Slovenia were the first to link their currencies to the euro ahead of monetary union after the EU's 2004 expansion, are not yet ready, the sources told Reuters.  

Slovenia, a small country to the south of Austria, already meets the criteria for euro membership -- a stable currency, low inflation and low budget deficits. But procedural quirks could delay the process and Austria is trying to remove them.  

"This should not be delayed just because of bureaucratic obstacles," one of the sources said. "They have done what they had to do, they are ready now."  

Austrian Finance Minister Karl-Heinz Grasser wants to decide about Slovenia under his country's EU presidency in the first half of the year. He will bring up the issue at next week's meeting of euro zone finance ministers, the sources said.  

Austria favours bringing forward to May the convergence reports written by the European Central Bank and the European Commission, in which they assess whether Slovenia meets the requirements for joining the 12-nation currency club.  

"The ECB has said it is ready to bring forward the report," another source said. "It looks as if the way is free for Slovenia to enter the euro in January 2007," the source said.  

Technically, a decision on Slovenia can only be made after it has been in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) that links the Slovene tolar to the euro for two years -- proving it can remain stable against the euro over that time period.  

Since Slovenia joined ERM-2 in late June 2004, a May recommendation on its readiness would be too early for the assessment. But this limit has been bent before.  

The ECB in 1998 issued a convergence report on Italy and Finland roughly six months before their two-year periods ended and said their currencies had been broadly stable without the need for intervention and were expected to remain so.  

READY  

Slovenia's central bank and finance ministry have both said the former Yugoslav country is ready for euro entry next year.  

When Slovenia joined the exchange rate mechanism the central parity of the tolar was set at 239.64 to the euro. It has been stable since.  

The country meets euro entry requirements for public debt, budget deficit and interest rates and in November managed to bring its inflation down to the maximum level allowed for those who want to adopt the euro.  

However, neither Lithuania and Estonia currently meet the euro criteria, European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Joaquin Almunia said on Thursday, and Estonia has already said it would rather wait.  

"If the assessment were made today, with the (inflation) numbers published by Eurostat this morning, neither Estonia nor Lithuania would meet the criterion," Almunia said.

title: First Year of ERM II Smooth for Slovenia
text:
Ljubljana, 18 June (STA) - It will be one year on 28 June since Slovenia  

joined the ERM II exchange rate mechanism, the waiting room for the euro.  

There have been no shake-ups so far: the exchange rate is steadily  

hovering around the central parity rate of SIT 239.64 per euro, and the  

central bank has had to intervene only once on the monetary market.  

"The Bank of Slovenia assesses the first year in the ERM II as successful.  

Economic growth, the situation in individual markets and preserved  

macroeconomic balances confirm that the preceding adjustment to the  

business conditions maintained in Europe by the European Central Bank was  

sustainable," central bank Vice-Governor Andrej Rant told STA.  

The exchange rate has remained close to the central parity rate throughout  

the year. The market rate was at SIT 239.54 on Friday and has been just  

below the parity rate since the end of April. According to central bank

data, the average gap between the market and parity rates has been 0.01%.  

The bank intervened on the market just once, one month after ERM II entry,  

when it sold foreign exchange to respond to rate growth.  

According to Rant, "this intervention arose from a need for a signal that  

the existing concept of exchange rate policy had indeed been brought to an  

end with Slovenia's entry in the ERM II." He says the banks were initially  

complacent, so they were given the signal.  

Slovenia intends to introduce the euro on 1 January 2007 according to the  

"big bang" scenario of overnight changeover. Banks will accept tolar bills  

until February 2007, while the central bank will impose no limitations.  

The reason why Slovenia opted for this scenario is the good experience  

that it had when Yugoslav dinars were replaced first by coupons and then  

by tolars in the early 90s. Moreover, the ECB has assessed that two months  

of dual legal tender in the 12 members that introduced the euro in 2002 was  

too long.  

To be eligible for the euro, Slovenia has to stay in the ERM II for  

another year and keep the exchange rate within plus or minus 15% of the  

central parity rate. Moreover, it has to fulfil the convergence criteria  

of low inflation, public debt and interest rates.  

Efforts to meet the criteria have been successful so far, except for  

inflation, which is only slowly coming down to the desired level. In May,  

inflation was 0.9 percentage points above the Maastricht threshold for  

that month.  

Yet the central bank is confident that inflation will be curbed  

sufficiently in time. "The forecasts of the Bank of Slovenia as well as  

other domestic and foreign institutions show that Slovenia will meet the  

inflation criterion in the reference period," Rant said.  

While inflation is the only criterion that Slovenia is yet to fulfil, the  

one-year reference period starting in June will be challenging  

nevertheless. The EU has noted that figures are not all that counts: the  

country's overall economic condition will also undergo thorough scrutiny.  

According to Rant, the second year in the ERM II will require close  

monitoring of wages and productivity. "The occurrence of a negative gap  

between the two is not a good sign," he emphasised. The focus will  

therefore be on current actions in ensuring the stability of public  

finances and managing labour costs.  

"Considering the uncertain oil prices, cost management is especially  

important and the changed economic conditions with forecasts of lower  

economic growth in Europe will be a challenge for public finances. Their  

flexibility could be put to a test," Rant added.  

Slovenia is gearing up for the euro in other areas as well. Companies do  

not expect any major shocks, as most are already doing business with  

eurozone countries. Moreover, over 60 percent of all exports end up in the  

EU.  

Indeed, businessmen expect benefits rather then difficulties, notably  

lower overhead costs, lower risk and greater attraction for foreign  

investment. Some problems are expected in the public and service sectors,  

especially retail.  

A heated debate has been under way about double pricing. Retailers  

initially insisted that double price tags are out of the question until  

the exchange rate is cemented, but this is theoretically possible only  

after the two-year ERM II period expires.  

The government and the Bank of Slovenia have come up with a solution that  

they believe will provide sufficient information for consumers while not  

putting too much pressure on retailers: price labels will include euros as  

of March 2006 according to the central parity rate, while double price tags  

will remain in place six months after the changeover to the euro.

title: DJ INTERVIEW: Slovene Central Bk: New Govt Must Stay Course
text:
LJUBLJANA, Sep 30, 2004 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

(This story was originally published Wednesday)  

By Nick Carey Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

Whichever party wins Slovenia's general elections Oct. 3 must stick to the country's agreed fiscal policy or risk failure to join the single European currency, the Slovene central bank governor told Dow Jones Newswires. "Any loosening of fiscal policy would be the greatest threat to our prospects of adopting the euro," Mitja Gaspari said earlier this week. "I would be very disappointed in any government that took that path." Gaspari also called on any future government to create fiscal reserves as the Slovene economy picks up after several years of healthy but unremarkable growth, and said he prefers to maintain a restrictive interest rate policy for as long as it's feasible. Slovenia entered the European exchange rate mechanism known as ERM2 - June 27, and is aiming to adopt the common European currency in 2007. Slovenia, which broke away the from former Yugoslav Republic in 1991 and has a population of just 2 million, joined the European Union May 1. Two other small new E.U. members, Estonia and Lithuania, joined ERM2 on the same day. Part of the logic behind the move is that the currencies of these small countries are particularly vulnerable to speculation, making the euro a more stable bet for business and trade. The Slovene central exchange parity rate agreed on with the European Central Bank is 239.64 tolar to the euro. The tolar has remained within 0.2% of that rate - the maximum fluctuation band is 15% - since late June. Gaspari said the central bank made one small intervention in July to maintain parity, but declined to comment on the size of that intervention. The general elections to be held in Slovenia this Sunday are expected to be a near-run thing. After 12 years as the main partner in successive coalition governments, the left-leaning Liberal Democrats of Slovenia, or LDS, face a serious challenge from the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party, or SDS. The country's main daily Delo gives SDS 21.5% of the vote, just 0.2 percentage points ahead of LDS, although polling agency GfK Gral-Iteo puts LDS at 16.6%, 3.6 points ahead of SDS. Either way, a close race is predicted. LDS' onetime lead of 10 percentage points has evaporated in recent weeks. Gaspari said the election promises of the main parties are irresponsible, as they would require significant increases in spending. Slovenia's fiscal deficits for 2004 and 2005 are expected to reach around 2% of gross domestic product, within the 3% GDP limit set by the Maastricht criteria for adopting the euro. "Any changes to fiscal policy would be counterproductive and would result in speculative attacks on the tolar," he said. The Slovene central bank, he added, is 100% committed to the euro adoption agreement brokered with the current government. Gaspari said one potential obstacle that must be overcome is reducing inflation. Although price rises have slowed from 9% in 2000 to an expected level of 3.5% this year, Gaspari said inflation will have to go lower if the country is to gain European Central Bank approval to adopt the euro. Under ERM2, Slovenia's inflation must be no higher than the average of the three lowest inflation rates in the euro zone, plus 1.5%. That currently gives a figure of around 2.5%. Gaspari said he expects inflation to fall to 3% next year, but that it may not reach 2.5% by the end of 2006, particularly if oil prices stay high. "Whether or not we're allowed to adopt the euro will be a matter for the ECB," he said. "Our task is to get as close as possible and then take it from there." Interest rates in Slovenia are higher than in the euro zone, with the central bank's key 60-day tolar bill rate at 4%, in comparison with the ECB's 2% key rate. The central bank last cut rates by 25 basis points in mid-June. Although the country's economy is beginning to take off, Gaspari said he is reluctant to raise interest rates any time soon. The Slovene economy picked up in the second quarter, with GDP growth of 4.6% recorded by the country's statistical office, up from 3.7% in the first quarter. Gaspari predicts GDP growth of 4% for the year, up from 2.5% in 2003 as the euro-zone economies gather steam. Almost 70% of Slovenia's trade is with other E.U. member states. Slovenia is the richest of all the new E.U. members, with an average monthly salary of around EUR800. Central bank Web site:  http://www.bsi.si("http://www.bsi.si")

-By Nick Carey, Dow Jones Newswires; 42 0 22 108 5272; nick.carey@dowjones.com

title: Gaspari: Inflation Rate to Drop below 3% Next Year
text:
Koper, 06 September (STA) - If Slovenia wants to introduce the euro in two  

years, it will first have to meet all the relevant Maastricht criteria, and  

inflation is still quite a significant problem, Bank of Slovenia governor  

Mitja Gaspari said at a meeting of businessmen from the coastal region on  

Monday.  

Due to high oil prices, Slovenia's inflation rate stood at an annual 3.7  

percent in August, which is more than had been expected, Gaspari observed.  

Next year Slovenia's inflation rate is expected to drop below 3 percent,  

provided there are no major price increases and surprises on the market,  

Gaspari went on to say.  

Now that Slovenia is in the ERM II, it is to face two key periods of  

verification of the Maastricht standards, namely in May and June 2005 and  

2006, Gaspari pointed out.  

According to the Maastricht criteria, the inflation rate of EU member  

states that want to introduce the euro must equal that of three members  

with the lowest inflation rate.  

Slovenia and some other countries though believe that it would be more  

logical to adapt to the inflation rate represented by the euro, as the new  

member states are joining a system with a common central bank, whose aim is  

to keep the annual inflation rate around two percent.  

"It is about the relationship between big and small countries. The big  

ones set the rules, and the small ones must respect them," Gaspari said.  

Our entry in the ERM II affects the rate of the tolar, which must be  

stable without major or too frequent interventions on the part of the  

central bank, Gaspari explained, adding that the Bank of Slovenia has only  

intervened once so far.  

According to the central bank governor, Slovenia's preparations for the  

euro are being quite efficient, the government, the Bank of Slovenia, the  

Bank Association of Slovenia and the Chamber of Commerce having drafted a  

good project for the introduction of the euro.  

Participation in the project is expected by the Slovenian Consumers'  

Association, as the new currency will be especially important for them.  

Gaspari in fact hopes that prices could start being marked in tolars and  

euros as soon as possible, so that people can start getting used to the  

new currency.

title: Signs of Slovenian success in steadying tolar-Buba.
text:
FRANKFURT, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Slovenia is having some success in halting its currency depreciation, which is important to the country's future adoption of the euro, the Bundesbank said on Monday.    

 Slovenia joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism ERM-2 in June, linking its tolar in a trading band against the euro to test whether it can keep the currency stable for at least two years before converting to the euro.    

 The tolar has depreciated a little, prompting central bankintervention.    

 "It will be decisive for Slovenia's successful participation in ERM-2 whether the depreciating trend of the tolar against the euro can be credibly broken," the Bundesbank said in its August monthly report.    

 "The first signs are thoroughly encouraging, even if the time period under consideration so far is very short," it added.    

 Slovenia, along with Baltic EU members Estonia and Lithuania, joined ERM-2 on June 27. The three were among 10 countries, mainly in central Europe, that joined the EU in May this year.    

 Slovenia set a central parity of 239.64 tolar to the euro when it joined ERM-2. ERM-2 members are required to intervene if their currencies appreciate or depreciate by more than 15 percent from the central parity against the euro.    

 The tolar had depreciated by 21 percent against the euro between the launch of the single currency in 1999 and Slovenia's joining ERM-2 in June, the Bundesbank said.    

 However, it noted that the tolar  had recently been trading at 240 to the euro, just 0.15 percent weaker than its central parity.    

 "The euro-tolar exchange rate therefore has been moving in a very narrow band so far, without having to make use of the permitted plus/minus 15 percent fluctuation margin around the central rate," the Bundesbank said.    

 The Bundesbank said that further tension-free development of the exchange rates of the tolar as well as the Estonian and Lithuanian currencies depended on those countries maintaining stability-oriented economic policies, particularly for government budgets, and carrying out structural reforms.    

Slovenia's central bank late last month intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time to support the tolar.    

 One currency trader said he saw the intervention more as a training manoeuvre and said the central bank was trying to defend an unofficial and self-imposed 0.2 percent band for the tolar.

title: News Roundup - Tuesday, 27 July
text:
Ljubljana, 27 July (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Tuesday,  

27 July:  

POLITICS  

BERLIN, Germany - International topics were at the forefront of Tuesday's  

talks between Foreign Minister Ivo Vajgl and his German counterpart  

Joschka Fischer. As Vajgl told STA, the pair focused on bilateral  

cooperation in the EU, issues related to the EU's common security and  

foreign policy, the future of OSCE, the Middle East and the Western  

Balkans. Relations between Slovenia and Germany are problem-free, while  

cooperation in economy, politics and culture has been developing well,  

Vajgl said he and his counterpart established. According to him, Germany  

supports Slovenia's admission to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation  

and Development. The minister also said he proposed signing a bilateral  

accord on free movement of labour.  

BERN, Switzerland - Slovenia and Switzerland signed agreements on fighting  

organised crime, the return of illegal residents, and deployment of  

liaison officers, as Interior Minister Rado Bohinc met his Swiss  

counterpart Cristoph Blocher in Bern on Tuesday. As Minister Bohinc told  

STA, the agreements will further upgrade cooperation between the Slovenian  

and Swiss police, making it more organised and efficient, as they will  

enable a faster and direct exchange of information. According to Bohinc,  

Slovenia as well as the countries to its north and west are exposed to  

criminal activities of the so-called Balkan route, including human, drugs  

and arms trafficking.  

PODGORICA, Serbia-Montenegro - Minister of Labour, Family and Social  

Affairs Vlado Dimovski is visiting Montenegro Tuesday and Wednesday at the  

invitation of his counterpart Slavoljub Stijepovic. The Labour Ministry  

says the purpose of the visit is to exchange experience and boost  

bilateral cooperation. Dimovski is expected to outline Slovenia's activity  

in the areas he is responsible for, in particular the country's experience  

in attaining EU standards in labour, family and social affairs, as well as  

employment and labour market policies. The two sides are further expected  

to share experiences with reforms, social security, pension and disability  

insurance. The visit is moreover seen as Slovenia's contribution to help  

Montenegro to promptly join the EU, the Labour Ministry stated in a press  

release.  

LJUBLJANA - Responding to an invitation by Foreign Minister Ivo Vajgl,  

head of the government of the Italian border region Friuli-Venezia Giulia  

Riccardo Illy is due to arrive in Slovenia on Wednesday for talks  

dominated by problems faced by both ethnic minorities, transport issues  

and cross border cooperation. According to the Foreign Ministry, the  

purpose of the visit is to confirm the close relations between both sides  

and set the guidelines for future cooperation. Relations took on a new  

dimension with Slovenia's accession to the EU, offering new opportunities  

of taking cooperation to a higher level, the Foreign Ministry said in a  

press release prior to the visit.  

NOVO MESTO - Milos Kovacic, the outgoing CEO of the pharmaceutical company  

Krka, will stand at the parliamentary elections as the candidate of the  

ruling Liberal Democrats (LDS). As he told the press on Tuesday, "business  

diplomacy" will be very important for Slovenia in the coming years if the  

country wants to be successful in the EU, adding he had rich experience as  

he has been at the helm of Krka for 20 years. Gregor Golobic, the chair of  

the LDS council, refused to say whether there will be more company heads  

on the LDS list at the autumn elections. He said that talks with potential  

candidates were still underway and that the list would be completed by the  

end of August.  

LJUBLJANA - Parliament Speaker Feri Horvat on Tuesday received Austrian  

Ambassador to Slovenia Ferdinand Mayrhofer-Gruenbuehl, thanking him for  

Austria's support in Slovenia's EU integration and for the swift aid  

offered in the wake of the Posocje earthquake earlier in July, the  

parliament said. The cooperation between Austria and Slovenia is well  

underway in all fields, particularly in economy. Horvat pointed out that  

bilateral trade amounts to almost EUR 2bn and that Austria is the biggest  

foreign investor in Slovenia, the parliament wrote in a press release.  

BUSINESS & ECONOMY  

LJUBLJANA - The mayor of the biggest financial centre in Europe said that  

Slovenia could act as a springboard for financial institutions wishing to  

do business in SE Europe. According to Robert Finch, the Lord Mayor of the  

City of London, there are many opportunities for cooperation between  

Slovenia and London City. Speaking at Tuesday's press conference after  

meeting PM Anton Rop, Finance Minister Dusan Mramor and Bank of Slovenia  

Governor Mitja Gaspari, Finch said the two sides should work for  

harmonisation in trade and greater cooperation between financial  

institutions. He said he would like to see London City involved in any  

possible second wave of privatisation in Slovenia, adding it was important  

to establish how London City could participate in the development of the  

Slovenian economy.  

LJUBLJANA - The Bank of Slovenia has intervened on the currency market for  

the first time since Slovenia entered the ERM II exchange rate mechanism,  

a grooming phase for the adoption of the euro. The bank sold euros - 20  

million according to some reports - in line with ERM II regulations, STA  

learnt from the central bank. Central bank officials would not elaborate,  

but said the move was nothing out of the ordinary.Slovenia's central bank

responded to the growth of the euro noted over the past week, the public  

radio broadcaster, Radio Slovenija, said. Analysts believe the sum in  

question is not substantial.  

LJUBLJANA - A day after appointing Marko Simoneti as the head of the  

Ljubljana Stock Exchange (LJSE), the supervisory board of the LJSE came  

out to say that Simoneti was the best choice. According to Zdenko  

Podlesnik, the head of the LJSE supervisory board, Simoneti was chosen  

unanimously to replace outgoing LJSE director Drasko Veselinovic. Simoneti  

already resigned as a supervisory board member in order to assume the new  

post on 1 January 2005. According to Podlesnik, the major challenge in the  

future will be the development of the Ljubljana Stock Exchange. "Among  

other things, services comparable with that on foreign stock markets will  

have to be phased in."  

LJUBLJANA - A day after the management of the Slovenian Railways boasted  

upbeat half-year business figures with profits of EUR 2.55m, the utility's  

trade union said Tuesday that workers had been forced to work extra hours  

not envisaged in the collective agreement. The trade union highlighted in  

today's press release that workers were forced to work 40 or 50 extra  

hours per month due to lack of labour force. Moreover, not all workers are  

able to take a break during a working day, while their working hours are  

not in line with the collective agreement, according to the union.  

LJUBLJANA - The Italian laboratory that examined bees found poisoned  

earlier in July has not found any traces of the substance contained in the  

disputed Gaucho pesticide but discovered the presence of two other  

substances, STA was told by the Agriculture Ministry, which will reveal  

the findings to the press on Friday. One substance was found from bees  

killed in the coastal region and a different one was detected in bees  

killed in the NW region of Gorenjsko, said Marina Rojko, the spokesperson  

at the Agriculture Ministry. The Veterinary Administration (VURS) is  

currently drafting conclusions, said Rojko, adding that veterinarians are  

to meet with beekeepers over the matter.  

LJUBLJANA - There were a total of 12,291 job vacancies in Slovenian at the  

end of 2003, up 5.7 percent compared with a year earlier. This is stated  

in the first vacancies statistics report, released by the national  

Statistics Office to align its methodology with that of Eurostat. The  

report says most vacancies were available in manufacturing (3,109), retail  

(1,898) and construction (1,851). Quite a few vacancies were also in  

financial services (212) and public administration (271), while only four  

jobs were available in fisheries and only 11 in private households  

employing staff.  

LJUBLJANA - The benchmark SBI 20 index gained 32.07 points or 0.7 percent  

on Tuesday to close the day at 4,610.47 points.  

LJUBLJANA - Optimism continued to prevail on the Ljubljana Stock Exchange,  

with the benchmark SBI 20 index gaining 32.07 points (0.7 percent) to  

close Tuesday's trading at 4,610.47 points. Despite the summer calm,  

volumes were moderate, amounting to SIT 1.04bn (EUR 4.34m), of which 40  

percent was done in four package deals.  

ARTS & CULTURE  

LJUBLJANA - A music concert by the Slovenian band Bast opened the  

traditional summer Trnfest Festival on Tuesday evening at KUD France  

Preseren, an independent cultural centre in Ljubljana. Over a hundred  

events are scheduled to take place until 31 August, all free of charge.  

One of the most popular open-air events in Ljubljana, which last year  

attracted some 40,000 visitors, will offer music concerts, theatre  

performances and literary readings, exhibitions, films, a special  

programme for children and the international Emona Promenade.  

VIENNA, Austria - A novel by Slovenian writer Lojze Kovacic, who passed  

away earlier this year, tops the list of ten best novels composed by the  

Austrian public broadcaster ORF for August. "Die Zugereisten", the German  

translation of the novel "Prisleki" (The Newcomers), has been published by  

the Klagenfurt-based Drava publisher. In this autobiographical novel,  

Kovacic depicts his childhood - a life of poverty and misery. Fantasy and  

imagination are strongly at work in the perception of the young Lojzek,  

who in 1938 suddenly finds himself in Slovenia, the homeland of his  

father. The novel has already won acclaim at home; critics have namely  

selected it the novel of the 20th century.  

CRIME  

IVANCNA GORICA - A major source of water for a small Slovenian region is  

under threat after hundreds of litres of dangerous chemicals were dumped  

in its vicinity on Sunday. Police apprehended a 24-year-old man on Sunday  

after he was found dumping several drums containing an unknown substance  

in the vicinity of the Globocec spring on Sunday. The suspect supposedly  

slashed the barrels open and more than 1,000 litres of various substances  

are said to have leaked out. Tests carried out so far have shown no signs  

that the spring has been contaminated, although environmental experts say  

that it could take days for contamination to show.  

OBREZJE - In the latest drug bust on Slovenia's border with Croatia,  

customs officials seized 28.6 kilograms of heroin that was supposedly  

headed to Germany. Customs officers discovered the drug stash in a van  

driven by two Bosnian citizens who tried to cross into Slovenia at the  

Obrezje border crossing last Thursday, customs officials told the press on  

Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 1-Slovenian cbank  intervenes  for first time since ERM-II.
text:
LJUBLJANA, July 27 (Reuters) - Slovenia's central bank said it had intervened to support the tolar in the domestic currency market on Tuesday for the first time since joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) last month as a step towards adopting the euro.  

"There was an intervention and the central bank has been selling foreign exchange," Gordana Pipan, spokeswoman for the Bank of Slovenia, told Reuters.  

"This was the first intervention of the central bank on the open foreign exchange market (since ERM-2 entry), in line with the concept explained at Slovenia's entry into ERM-2," she added  

The Bank of Slovenia said it had sold foreign currency but declined to elaborate. Traders said the bank had sold 20 million euros.  

"There was some more buying than selling (of euros) last week and the exchange rate rose. So it is a bit surprising that this came today, I would have expected it yesterday or last week," one trader at Bank Austria-Creditanstalt said.  

"I see this (intervention) more as a training manoeuvre, since the central bank is trying to defend the unofficial and self-imposed 0.2 percent band for the tolar," he added.  

The tolar was trading at 239.89/240.01 at 1301 GMT. The central parity of Slovenia's currency under ERM-II was set at 239.640 tolars per euro.  

The European Central Bank set its upper and lower intervention rates for the tolar at 275.586 tolar per euro and 203.694 tolar, respectively.  

European Union newcomers Slovenia, Estonia and Lithuania joined the ERM-2 at the end of June and became the first of 10 new EU members to join ERM-2, the block's waiting room for the euro which they plan to adopt at the start of 2007.
