title: News Roundup - Tuesday, 28 January.
text:
Ljubljana, 28 January (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Tuesday, 28 January: 

 LJUBLJANA - After the coalition-proposed motion on the consultative EU and NATO referendums is expected to be dabated in parliament either tommorrow or Thursday, the government and the opposition are still engaged in talks in a bid to reach a consensus of all parties, a POP TV report said. A compromise would involve two changes to the Constitution, TV Slovenija reported, and added that legal experts have already gathered to draft a compromise deal. Speaker of the Parliament Borut Pahor could neither deny nor confirm the TV reports about the talks. Furthermore, the public broadcaster TV Slovenija said that MPs are expected to discuss the calling of both referendums, scheduled for 23 March, on Thursday rather than late tommorrow evening. Head of the LDS deputy faction Tone Anderlic, however, told STA that the motions could well be debated as early as tomorrow. LJUBLJANA - The coalition SLS expects the Defence Ministry to produce a detailed study of both scenarios of Slovenia's integration into NATO, namely one if Slovenia's chooses NATO membership and the other if it decides to remain outside the Alliance. The study should include the costs of both scenarios, SLS president Franci But told the press. According to But, citizens need to be informed about the exact cost of NATO membership and the impact it would have on the position of the country, which is part of the region where conflicts are frequent. The ministry should also explain what would happen to the professionalization of the armed forces in either scenario and how much neutrality would cost. LJUBLJANA - Slovenia has joined the EU's stance on the Iraqi crisis, reiterating that an efficient and complete disarmament of Iraq is the solution to the crisis, the Foreign Ministry, which is following the developments carefully and with concern, said in a press release. The country believes that the supreme authority to solve disputes in the international community is the UN Security Council, so Slovenia believes Iraq should fulfil its obligations stemming from UN Security Council resolutions. Meanwhile, a news report said that the U.S. has sent a second request to Slovenia to take part in a potential intervention in Iraq. According to POP TV, which quoted "well informed sources", the U.S. asked Slovenia in a "semi-official way" whether the country would be willing to offer additional, different form of expert help, namely experts in medicine, biological, chemical and nuclear weapons as well as IT experts. The most surprising request, according to the TV station, was that for translators for Arabic. LJUBLJANA - The coverage of the president's speech before the World Economic Forum in Davos, alleging that he warned that the referendum on Slovenia's accession to NATO might not succeed if the U.S. decides to take unilateral action against Iraq without the approval of the UN, stirred a lot of attention in Slovenia. Until the Davos forum press release summarising his statement, Slovenian officials never linked the issues of attack on Iraq and a NATO referendum, said the national TV Slovenija. To clarify any misunderstanding after the Davos press office apologised to the president's office earlier today for wrongly reporting on his statement, the state-owned TV network aired the relevant excerpt from President Janez Drnovsek's speech in Davos. At the forum's plenary session on trans-Atlantic relations, Drnovsek said that a unilateral U.S. action against Iraq "would certainly not help the partnership, and I must certainly say that it would not help me or our government in Slovenia to win the referendum on NATO...". LJUBLJANA - Irish Minister for Europe Dick Roche will be arriving for a one-day visit to Slovenia tomorrow for talks dominated by concerns of the future make-up of the soon-to-be enlarged EU. The issue is being debated within the European Convention, a forum responsible to draft a European Constitution by mid-year. The visiting minister is scheduled to hold talks with Foreign Minister Dimitrij Rupel, Europe Minister Janez Potocnik and head of the parliamentary foreign affairs commitee Jelko Kacin. LJUBLJANA - Macedonian Deputy Prime Minister Radmila Sekerinski is scheduled to pay a visit to Slovenia tomorrow. She is to be hosted by Europe Minister Janez Potocnik, who is to discuss with her Slovenia's experiences in accession to the EU. Slovenian authorities have said on several occasions that helping Balkan countries in their efforts to join the EU is an opportunity as well as duty for Slovenia as a soon-to-be EU member with vast experiences gained in the accession process. Sekerinski is first expected to hold talks with Slovenian Economics Minister Tea Petrin, followed on Wednesday afternoon with a meeting with Potocnik and Labour Minister Vlado Dimovski. A meeting with Parliament Speaker Borut Pahor is scheduled for Thursday. LJUBLJANA - Terms for the presidential function and the organisation of the president's office in Slovenia have been set in the bill on the presidential office, which was passed in 44-28 vote in parliament. The new act also defines the rights and privileges of former state presidents. The bill on reducing the consumption of alcohol was also passed today. Backed in a 37:12 vote, the new act is related to the fact that consumption of alcohol per capita ranks Slovenia at the top in the world, while harmful consequences of alcohol abuse are one of Slovenia's major health issues. LJUBLJANA - The non-parliamentary Environmental Movement Party (SEG) has joined the debate about the construction of a mosque in Ljubljana, stating that no religion should meddle with politics. "Religion in politics sows discord instead of building unity and arouses hatred instead of love," the party said, voicing its support for the construction of a mosque in Ljubljana. The commercial TV station POP TV meanwhile, reported yesterday that Muslim Mufti Osman Djogic quoted Saudi Arabia, Qatar, UAE and Turkey as the countries that could help by providing financial resources for the construction of a mosque. STRASBOURG - Slovenian parliament's permanent delegation to the Council of Europe (CoE) has addressed a letter to President of the CoE Parliamentary Assembly Peter Schieder, drawing his attention to the only round-the-clock radio programme of the Slovenian ethnic minority in Austria, which is to stop broadcasting due to a lack of funds. The delegation - currently attending the first part of the regular session of the CoE Parliamentary Assembly in Strasbourg - wanted to inform Schieder on the problem the Slovenian minority has in acquiring funds for Radio Dva. Schieder was also asked to help resolve the problem. The letter was handed over to Schieder by the head of Slovenian delegation Roman Jakic. LJUBLJANA - Croatia has sent to the Slovenian government the last request before arbitration to settle issues related to the jointly-owned N-plant in Krsko (NEK). The Croatian side is asking Slovenia to purchase Croatia's stake in NEK. That the request has been received was confirmed by the Slovenian Environment Ministry, which is to respond to the offer early next week. However, while the Slovenian government intends to study the document, it insists on the stance that all NEK-related issues have been adequately settled in the Slovenian-Croatian NEK agreement. The government will therefore try to get the accord ratified by the Slovenian parliament. The last Croatian attempt to resolve the NEK dispute with Slovenia before resorting to arbitration has been made because arbitration has to be called in not later than five years after the dispute has emerged, that is before 30 July 2003. LJUBLJANA - The council of the Bank of Slovenia confirmed amendments to the act on banking, which has already been forwarded to the Finance Ministry, and amended decrees on money transfers with abroad and reporting market players on securities trading. According to the central bank, the amended act also sets down new regulations on the acquisition of qualified stakes of foreign banks in Slovenian banks and vice versa. As a result of the changes to decree governing money transfers with banks abroad, Slovenians will be able to buy and sell foreign securities directly from 1 February, without having to go through a licensed Slovenia-based trader. The change has been made to comply with the EU accession agreement, which stipulates a four-year transitional period that expires on the first day of February. MARIBOR - It is good that the government has drafted a programme that enables more systematic monitoring of prices which are not directly influenced by the market, and has defined tax interventions in areas where this is required by a monopoly or oligopoly market situation. This is how Bank of Slovenia governor Mitja Gaspari assessed the government's anti-inflation programme for the daily Vecer. What is most important with the anti-inflation programme is that the government decided that the planned price increases will take place in proportion to the general price rise, Gaspari said in an interview for the Maribor-based daily. LJUBLJANA - The Economics Ministry earmarked EUR 31m to encourage the development of companies this year, EUR 15.6m of which have already been distributed to companies through public tenders to encourage entrepreneurship and competition. These are development encouragement and not classic state aids given to troubled companies, which is why the invitations for applications are intended for solid companies, particularly from the sectors vital for successful breakthrough on international markets, Economics Ministry State Secretary Mateja Mesl told the press yesterday. The amount allocated for development encouragement is higher that last year's, when EUR 20m were provided. LJUBLJANA - A delegation of the Polish Ministry for Infrastructure led by relevant minister and Deputy PM Marek Pol is to arrive for a three-day visit to Slovenia tommorrow upon the invitation of Transport Minister Jakob Presecnik. An agreement on sea transport is to be signed by both officials on Thursday. The delegations are to discuss the development of transport infrastructure, while the economic co-operation between the two countries in transport is also to be touched on, said Transport Ministry. Poland is a very important business partner of Slovenia's. According to the GZS figures, Poland holds the tenth place among importers of Slovenian goods, with a 2.6% share of Slovenia's total exports. It is also at the 17th place among exporters to Slovenia, with Polish goods making 1.4 percent of all Slovenian imports. KOPER - Istrabenz, a company which specialises in energy, tourism and investments, generated a net profit of EUR 14.3m in 2002, with revenues at EUR 37.6m, according to preliminary estimates. Istrabenz chairman Igor Bavcar told a press conference that the company is expected to earn EUR 19.9m this year, with a net profit of EUR 9.3m. The company, which has 16 subsidiaries, plans to expand its business in 2003, most notably to offer integral energy solutions and conduct real estate business. Two dependent companies will be set up to manage these businesses, each with a starting capital of about one million euros. The value of Istrabenz's real estate deals is expected to amount to EUR 25m in five years. SKOPJE - A court in Skopje is expected to decide by the end of January whether to issue a temporary injunction prohibiting owners of Macedonia's largest publishing house Nova Makedonija, the largest being Slovenian company Jug storitve, from exercising ownership rights over their stakes in the company, the Skopje-based newspaper Utrinski vesnik reported. According to the daily, this would freeze shares of Nova Makedonija, which Jug storitve purchased at a public privatisation tender last year, until the final solution of a dispute on one of the most compromised privatisation cases in the country. The Slovenian group has been facing troubles ever since it bought 70 percent of the publishing house for EUR 2.3m in September. LJUBLJANA - This year will be crucial for the leading Slovenian clothes maker Mura, which will have to reverse negative trends of the last three years, CEO Borut Meh told the daily Dnevnik. According to Meh, this will depend on the goodwill of the state, for which he believes it would be better to take part in helping the ailing Mura back on track rather than having to deal with social problems if the restructuring programme fails. Moving Mura's production into countries with cheaper workforce might seem the easiest solution, however this scenario would leave 5,000 or 4,000 people out of job in SE Slovenia, which is the country's poorest region, causing a major social problem both for the region and for the state. LJUBLJANA - Slovenia's tourism industry posted a three-percent rise in the number of foreign visitors and tourist nights. With a total of 2,158,240 tourists and 7,311,846 overnight stays registered in 2002, the "magic number" of two million tourists was beaten for the second year in a row. As head of Slovenian Tourist Board (STO) Bojan Meden told the press, last year was very successful, as revenues from tourism are expected to exceed one billion euros, according to unofficial business results. Most foreign visitors to Slovenia came from Italy, Germany, Austria and Croatia. The number of Slovenian tourists and tourist nights went down one percent last year with a total of 857,382 domestic visitors. LJUBLJANA - Slovenia's foreign exchange reserves totalled US$ 7.84bn at the end of November 2002, up US$ 843m from the previous month and up US$ 2.45bn over November 2001. Meanwhile, the country's foreign debt amounted to US$ 8.23bn, thus exceeding the foreign exchange reserves by US$ 391m. The bulk of all foreign exchange reserves, US$ 6.61bn, were held by the Bank of Slovenia, while the rest, US$ 1.23bn, was held by the commercial banks. Since the end of 2001, the reserves of the central bank increased by US$ 2.36bn, while those in commercial banks dropped by US$ 270m in the first eleven months of 2002. According to the central bank bulletin, the long-term foreign debt totalled US$ 8.12bn, while the short-term debt stood at US$ 112m. Over US$ 3bn of the long-term debt was public and state-guaranteed debt, while the remaining amount of around US$ 5bn was private debt. LJUBLJANA - The Ljubljana bourse engaged in modest trading, the volume of trade amounting to EUR 4.7m after 2,090 deals were made, including three package deals. Most indices dropped, including the benchmark SBI 20 index. The latter dropped by nearly 0.75 percent to 3,323.74 points. BREZICE - The Slovenian 16th century composer Iacobus Handl Gallus (1550-1591) is to receive special attention at the festival of classical music in the SE Slovenian town of Brezice. According to the festival director Klemen Ramovs, the major works works of Gallus - whop was a contemporary of Orlando di Lasso, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, Giovanni Gabrieli and Claude Monteverdi - are to be performed at the Brezice Festival in the next few years. The festival intends to become the European centre reviving and presenting Gallus's music. Gallus's motets are to be performed by soloists accompanied by old instruments.

title: News Roundup - Saturday, 14 September.
text:
Ljubljana, 14 September (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Saturday, 14 September: 

 BRATISLAVA - The co-operation between candidate countries for EU membership within the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) has definitely contributed to making them fit for the integration in the EU, said Slovenian PM Janez Drnovsek at the CEFTA summit in the Slovakian capital, which wound up with the signing of a joint declaration. Drnovsek, who has also met with his Hungarian counterpart Peter Medgyessy, believes that "just as CEFTA has served for the preparation of our countries to EU membership, so it will in the future". Drnovsek pointed out that Slovenia, which is to host next year's CEFTA summit, will try to maintain co-operation between signatory countries, while keeping CEFTA's door open for new members. At the end of next year, CEFTA is expected to lose some of its signatories - which currently include Slovenia, Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania - because all countries that are integrated into the EU have to give up all free trade agreements that do not involve the EU. NEW YORK - Slovenian Foreign Minister Dimitrij Rupel yesterday met with his Yugoslav counterpart Goran Svilanovic on the sidelines of the 57th UN General Assembly. The two discussed the development of bilateral relations, agreeing that a legal base is required in order to further them, particularly in economy. Rupel expressed support for Yugoslav efforts for membership in the Council of Europe. The Slovenian minister moreover met representatives of the American Jewish Committee at their request, and attended a working dinner of the Human Security Network, hosted by Austrian Foreign Minister Benita Ferrero-Waldner, as Austria currently chairs the initiative. MARIBOR - A lot of co-ordination will be necessary if the Swiss multinational Novartis actually takes over the Ljubljana-based drug maker Lek, believes the Bank of Slovenia Governor Mitja Gaspari. "If the central bank did not intervene on the market with such transactions as is Novartis's, tolar could gain as much as twenty percent in nominal terms, and such appreciation could not be endured," Gaspari told the daily Vecer. The co-ordination will be necessary also so as to prevent great oscillations on the foreign exchange market, Gaspari explained. Such sterilisation policy, which has to be carried out by the central bank to make the exchange policy relatively successful, also requires somewhat higher interest rates, Gaspari said. If the prices fail to steady at the same time, such policy of interest rates will be present for a longer period of time, Gaspari explained. LJUBLJANA - Slovenian agriculture is far from being unfit for the EU, Emil Erjavec, professor at the Biotechnical Faculty in Ljubljana and member of the negotiation group for Slovenia's accession to the EU, told the daily Delo. Farmers may have been even overly informed about what is expecting them, but the issue here is not only about the EU or EU integration, Erjavec thinks. Slovenian farmers will be increasingly exposed to market and capitalism laws, regardless of Slovenia's integration into the EU. Erjavec also said that at this moment what counts most for Slovenian agriculture is not so much the amount of subventions that it obtains, but rather the position of the Slovenian market and the competitive position of its food industry. LJUBLJANA - Slovenian oil traders Petrol and Istrabenz, which both export to Bosnia-Herzegovina, are quite satisfied with a decree issued by the Bosnian council of ministers by which the country will from now on import only liquid oil fuel that is in line with European standards. Since Petrol has been maintaining the requested quality standards for a long time now, the Ljubljana-based company expects the decree to increase its competition advantages on the Bosnian market, director of Petrol BH Oil Company Silvo Komar has told STA. The Bosnian subsidiary of Istrabenz, OMV Istrabenz BiH, has not yet examined the decree, but essentially the company thinks it is a positive move which will hopefully settle the circumstances on a rather difficult market. LJUBLJANA - The trading on the Ljubljana Stock Exchange last week took place under speculations about the announced takeover of the Slovenian pharmaceutical Lek by the Swiss multinational Novartis. Investors felt a bit uneasy because Bank Austria sold a lot of Lek shares, most of them in foreign ownership, below the announced takeover price of SIT 95,000 (EUR 416), as low as at SIT 87,800 (EUR 385). The benchmark SBI 20 index closed the week at 3,312.08 points, down 10.6 points (0.32 percent) over the previous week. The turnover amounted to EUR 51m. OBREZJE - Around 2,000 dead birds were discovered by Slovenian customs officers in an Italian van with a trailer at the Slovenian-Croatian border crossing Obrezje on Wednesday. A fowling piece was also found inside a double wall of the vehicle, the Slovenian Customs Administration said. According to the smugglers, the birds - protected by the 1979 Bern Convention on the conservation of European wildlife and natural habitats - were shot in the surroundings of Osijek, in eastern Croatia, where the two had been spending a hunting week.

title: Takeover of Lek will Require a Lot of Co-ordination,  Central Bank  Governor Says.
text:
Maribor, 14 September (STA) - A lot of co-ordination will be necessary if the Swiss multinational Novartis actually takes over the Ljubljana-based drug maker Lek, believes the Bank of Slovenia Governor Mitja Gaspari. "If the central bank did not intervene on the market with such transactions as is Novartis's, tolar could gain as much as twenty percent in nominal terms, and such appreciation could not be endured," Gaspari told the Saturday issue of the daily Vecer. 

 The co-ordination will be necessary also so as to prevent great oscillations on the foreign exchange market, Gaspari explained. Such sterilisation policy, which has to be carried out by the central bank to make the exchange policy relatively successful, also requires somewhat higher interest rates, Gaspari said. If the prices fail to steady at the same time, such policy of interest rates will be present for a longer period of time, Gaspari explained. The governor explained that the central bank had been in contact with banks ever since the announcement about the intended Lek takeover. On a technical level, the bank is also in contact with the potential bidder. The main reason for that is to explain how the system works, so as to make sure that the transaction - if it takes place - is carried out without difficulties, Gaspari said. "We also told the potential bidder in what way such a transaction cannot be carried out in Slovenia, as there has been some incomprehension," said Gaspari, adding that this was mainly about the currency and how the offer can be prepared. Commenting on the future of Slovenian banks, the central bank believes that the achieved share of foreign capital in banking is big enough, so that there is no need to further increase it substantially. The combination of domestic, foreign, private and public shares will gradually stabilise, according to the governor. Gaspari also touched on the announced preparation of a new privatisation programme of Slovenia's second largest bank, Nova Kreditna banka Maribor (NKBM). The central bank expects to be presented with the plans sometimes in autumn, to see whether they are in line with the views of the central bank about a stable functioning of the banking market. The central bank governor said the net inflow to Slovenia this year amounted to around EUR 500m. The transactions from Lek sale and the sale of a 34-percent of Nova Ljubljanska banka (NLB), Slovenia's largest bank, to the Belgian banking group KBC, will raise the share to that comparable to last year's, he explained. As for inflation movements, the Bank of Slovenia expects the government not to raise government-controlled prices substantially by the end of the year, which was agreed at a meeting in May. Gaspari believes that the inflation can still be cut to four percent by 2004, although there are some unknowns, such as the price of oil derivatives. "Therefore it is important that we do as few mistakes as possible. The time dimension has become essential - we are running out of time," he pointed out. Gaspari expects that next year already Slovenia will reach the point so as to be able to fix the exchange rate to the euro after EU accession. This will happen only if there are no substantial deviations from current movements and if the exchange depreciation steadies gradually, provided there are no unpredictable events. We expect the fixation could be reached in a year and a half. But, foremost, inflation rate must drop to four percent, Gaspari told Vecer.

title: Economic Expert Mencinger Blames Government for High Inflation.
text:
Ljubljana, 22 May (STA) - It is pointless to stop inflation by force as it is only the consequence of some other economic developments. In the case of Slovenia, it is chiefly the problem of growing expenses, as we usually distinguish between inflation of expenses and inflation of demand, economist Joze Menciger said in an interview for the national television and added that it was the government and its unsuccessful pay policy that is to blame for high inflation. 

 Mencinger, who is also the chancellor of the University of Ljubljana, does not believe it sensible to curb inflation by means of money supply. That would not be productive and it would also cause a stagnation. Since the Slovene central bank has been trying to help the net exporters by means of the exchange rate of the domestic currency, it has been doing what it can. "The blame is therefore fully on the part of the government," Mencinger said late on Tuesday commenting on the dispute between Economics Minister Tea Petrin and Governor of the Bank of Slovenia Mitja Gaspari on who is to blame for such a high inflation rate in Slovenia. In April the annual inflation rate stood at 8.4 percent. Mencinger does not think an intervention on the money market by the Bank of Slovenia necessary to stop a further increase in inflation. According to him, it is a well-konwn fact that ever since Slovenia became independent a decade ago, the central bank has been taking care of the relatively weak tolar and thus helped the exporters. "Inflation is related to money indeed, but in the long run. In the short run, the two factors are not related, especially in the transition economies," he explained. The central bank governor's forecast of a four-percent inflation rate in 2003 is attainable in Mencinger's opinion, but it will largely depend on movements in world oil prices. "Should these drop, his (Gaspari's) forecast holds true". Commenting on the announced budget supplement, Mencinger said that the adoption of the two-year budget plan was a nonsense, which was applauded by everybody. The government renounced fiscal policy in advance, and only three months later a budget supplement was announced. "I believe that the government has responded too quickly and, above all, nonsensically by suspending contracts for 25 days. That will only raise costs," Mencinger added in concern with the government decision to suspend the implementation of the budget for 25 days and stop assuming all new contractual obligations for budget-funded goods and services, subsidies, investments, and the purchase and construction of basic assets.

title: Review of the Slovene Economy - December 1999 to November 2000.
text:
Ljubljana, 09 December (STA) - Higher prices of oil and raw materials had a considerable impact on the economic conditions in the year 2000. Nevertheless, the economic trends were quite positive both in Slovenia and in the world. Worse trading conditions, a higher external debt and the lack of direct foreign investment in particular in the second half of the year, however, caused an imbalance in Slovenia's current payments, while the current deficit was up and got close to the record figures of 1999. Slovenia's foreign currency reserves fell below US$ 4 billion last August for the first time in the last three and a half years, while the external debt rose to US$ 5.78 billion. Due to the fluctuation of oil prices on the world market the government adopted in April a price-setting model for petrol and, in October, also for natural gas. 

 Slovenia continued the alignment of its legislation with EU standards. While insurance legislation was passed, the telecommunications bill, which should determine the rules of the game before Slovenia opens its telecommunications market for foreign competition in 2001, had less luck. Brussels criticised Slovenia for not having privatised banks, insurance companies and the biggest state-owned companies. In the year of political changes personnel replacements in state-owned companies and other state-run institutions were frequent. The attempt to merge the Port of Koper and the forwarding agent Intereuropa into a logistics centre, which would be one of the biggest in the Adriatic region, has failed. Still, in the autumn the Port of Koper and its partners were granted a licence for the management of the container berth in the Italian port of Trieste. A number of takeovers took place in the year 2000, in particular in the production of beverages, in the trade and dairy sectors as well as in 

 the chemical industry. 

 Slovenia's economic growth in 2000, previously expected to reach 4.75 percent, will probably be slightly lower. The inflation rate, however, will be higher than the planned 6.1 percent. Due to a number of unfavourable international factors it is likely to reach 8.9 percent. Slovenia's industrial production rose by 7.2 percent in the first ten months of 2000 in comparison with the same period of 1999. The unemployment rate was by 1.4 percent lower in September than a year before, reaching 11.7 percent. Measured at ILO standards it stood at just 6.7 percent. The average gross wages rose by 1.5 percent in real terms between January and September in comparison with the same period last year. 

 DECEMBER 1999 

 1st SEATTLE - A Slovene delegation, led by Minister of Economic Relations and Development Marjan Senjur, attended a WTO ministerial conference. 17th LJUBLJANA - The amended veterinary act took effect. 21st ZAGREB - Meetings of the Slovene-Croatian commission for economic cooperation and the joint committee for the implementation of the free trade agreement. 22nd LJUBLJANA - The price of electricity for households rose two by percent, while that for industry remained unchanged. 22nd LJUBLJANA - Joze Lenic was appointed Director of the Pension Management Fund. 23rd LJUBLJANA - Marjan Rekar was appointed President of the Slovene Development Corporation (SRD). 28th LJUBLJANA - The amended act on tax procedure took effect. 29th MARIBOR - Mirko Zagar, TAM's trustee in bankruptcy, and the Consortium of Purchasers of TAm's property signed a contract to sell the entire TAM's property for SIT 9.4 billion (US$ 39 million). 

 JANUARY 

 1st LJUBLJANA - Slovenia liberalised its trade in agriculture and food products with all CEFTA members. 1st LJUBLJANA - The dairy Gorenjska mlekarna became a part of the dairy Ljubljanske mlekarne. 6th LJUBLJANA - The government adopted the direct investment promotion programme for 2000. 14th MARIBOR - The banks SKB and NKBM signed a letter of intent to merge, but as the NKBM failed to privatise the plan was not realized and the SKB began searching for a new strategic partner. 17th KRANJ - Rubber goods producer Sava acquired a majority stake in Chemo. 21st LJUBLJANA - The parliament passed the 2000 budget. 22nd LJUBLJANA - The act on the supervision of state aids took effect. 23rd LJUBLJANA - The key provisions of the act on financial operations of companies took effect. The provisions set down the measures that have to be taken in case of insolvency as well as the guarantees for capital adequacy. They also stipulate personal responsibility of the management. 27th DAVOS - Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek attended 30th World Economic Forum. 30th PRISTINA - A Slovene government and business delegation visited Kosovo. 

 FEBRUARY 

 1st LJUBLJANA - The veterinary and sanitary inspection rules took effect. 9th LJUBLJANA - Slovenia and Hungary signed an agreement on the use of the Port of Koper and logistics centres. 10th LJUBLJANA - The Centre for Tourist Promotion of Slovenia was renamed the National Tourist Association of Slovenia (SNTO). 27th LJUBLJANA - The Slovene Development Corporation organised a transfer of property to the authorized investment companies for bridging the privatisation gap. The gap was reduced from SIT 158.1 billion (US$ 658 million) to SIT 76.3 billion (US$ 316 million) in the year 2000. 

 MARCH 

 3th LJUBLJANA - The parliament defeated a motion of interpellation against Finance Minister Mitja Gaspari, which was proposed by the SKD and the SLS. 3rd LJUBLJANA - The acts on the privatisation of insurance companies and on the insurance industry took effect. The latter opens the insurance market for foreign competition. 8th ROME - Slovenia and Italy signed agreements on investment promotion and on cooperation in education, science and culture. 9th MURSKA SOBOTA - The dairy Pomurske mlekarne confirmed the acquisition of the dairy Mlekarne Ptuj. 22nd SKOPJE - Soft drinks producer Fructal acquired a majority stake in the Macedonian producer of fruit juices Konzeks. 28th MOKRICE - A meeting of Slovene and Croatian negotiators for an inter-state agreement on the Krsko nuclear power plant. 

 APRIL

title: News Roundup - Monday, 13 November.
text:
Ljubljana, 13 November (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Monday, 13 November: 

 LJUBLJANA - Slovene President Milan Kucan is due to propose a candidate for prime minister to the parliament on Tuesday, Kucan's office said in a press release following his consultations with representatives of parliamentary parties. Tomorrow morning Kucan will meet the leader of the Liberal Democracy of Slovenia (LDS) Janez Drnovsek, the most likely candidate for a new prime minister given the distribution of seats in parliament after the October general elections, and a nearly completed coalition talks. 

 MARSEILLES - Slovene Foreign Minister Lojze Peterle and Defence Minister Janez Jansa attended a ministerial session of the Western European Union (WEU). This will probably be the last ministerial session of the WEU, as the majority of the tasks of this organisation are being progressively taken over by the European Union. Peterle and Jansa announced at the session Slovenia's intention to offer Slovene forces for the establishment of European military forces at the conference for the establishment of EU forces on 21 November in Brussels. 

 LJUBLJANA - Elected to the post of Speaker of the National Assembly last Friday, the leader of the third largest parliamentary party, Borut Pahor, stressed in an interview for Delo that Parliament is no front, but a sovereign branch of power, and should consolidate its position in politics. ZLSD leader Pahor, a 37-year old political scientist who has been an MP for ten years, added: "I find it wrong that after ten years of parliamentary democracy some still strongly underestimate Parliament as a domain in which power is created." 

 WARSAW - Foreign Ministries of Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Slovenia took part in a consultation organized by the Foreign Ministry of Poland, holding this year's presidency of Visegrad countries, reported the Slovene Embassy from the Polish capital. The participants mainly discussed situation in South Eastern Europe and the potential for regional co-operation. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Bank of Slovenia will stop intervening on the foreign exchange market by fixing the base exchange rate and the maximum difference. Commercial banks will be able to set selling and buying rates freely as of 14 November, the central bank said. The Bank of Slovenia started changing the base exchange rate for the euro and the maximum difference between the highest selling rate and the lowest buying rate on 27 to direct the desired growth of the exchange rate. 

 LJUBLJANA - One of the major Zagreb-based Croatian banks is allegedly interested in merging with the Slovene commercial bank SKB, according to paper Finance. The Croatian bank would like to merge with the SKB as a member of an international finance group. Two most important Croatian banks, Zagrebacka banka and Privredna banka, both have close links with international financial institutions. The chairwoman of the SKB board, Cvetka Selsek, recently said that several foreign financial institutions were interested in the SKB, but did not wish to discuss potential merger details. 

 LJUBLJANA - Slovenia's exports increased by 0.6 percent to US$ 773.59 million while imports dropped by 1.8 percent to US$ 831.31 million in September over September 1999. The deficit totaled US$ 57.71 million, while exports covered 93.1 percent of imports in September, the National Statistical Office said. Preliminary data provided by the Office show a 20 percent increase in exports and a 40 percent increase in imports in September over a month before. In the first nine months Slovenia's exports increased by 3.5 percent to US$ 6.51 billion and imports by 1.8 percent to US$ 7.55 billion so that the trade gap stood at US$ 1.04 billion and the exports-imports ratio at 86.2 percent. 

 LJUBLJANA - Prices of oil derivatives will drop on Tuesday. Retail prices of motor fuel will decrease by approximately six percent, reported both Slovene oil companies, Petrol and OMV Istrabenz. A decrease in retail prices of four to six percent will also affect diesel and fuel oil. 

 LONDON - Slovenia's promotion at the London Tourist Bourse, a major international event of its kind which kicked off today, is focussing on trekking in the Julian Alps and the Triglav National Park, backed by a presentation of a record-breaking achievement accomplished by Slovene Alpine skier Davo Karnicar, who has recently skied down the Mount Everest. The bourse has also been visited by Slovene Minister of Small Business and Tourism Janko Razgorsek, who took this opportunity to hold a series of informal meetings with his counterparts and representatives of the world tourist industry. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Slovene share index, SBI 20, dropped 0.35 percent to stand at 1722.71 points at today's close. (konec)eho/ep STA022 2000-11-13/18:58.

title: Weekly Review of the Slovene Economy from 28 October to 3 November.
text:
Ljubljana, 05 November (STA) - Slovene motorists experienced what is becoming a familiar story this year: another increase in the prices of petrol. The tenth rise in petrol prices this year alone, saw most types of petrol, with the exception of diesel and heating oil, increase in price by a good 5 percent. The reason behind all of this was the rising U.S. dollar, which, did however, fall SIT 11.17 during the week to stand at SIT 239.88. Following all the increases in the price of petrol, among other things, Slovenia's year-to-year inflation in October stood at 9 percent. 

 CHRONOLOGY: MONDAY, 30 October LJUBLJANA - The Bank of Slovenia once again intervened on the foreign exchange market in a bid to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank expressed belief that the growth of the exchange rate was still too low. The base exchange rate was fixed at SIT 210.40 (previous Friday it was set at SIT 210.25) for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. The measure took effect on Thursday. 

 WEDNESDAY, 1 November LJUBLJANA - Following several years of negotiations, the Slovene Steelworks (SZ) became an associate member of the European Confederation of Iron and Steel Industries (Eurofer). As STA had found out from a member of the SZ board, the chief advantage of membership is being in continuous contact with 95 percent of West European steel makers associated in the Brussels-based confederation. LJUBLJANA - The price of natural gas from the fixed underground network increased to stand at SIT 41.07 from SIT 39.48. The rise in the U.S. dollar stands behind this latest increase. This price increase only affected industry and distributors and did not concern household users. 

 THURSDAY, 2 November LJUBLJANA - Prices of petrol increased at filling stations around Slovenia, it was reported from the two largest petrol companies in Slovenia, Petrol and OMV Istrabenz. The latest price increase, which saw the price of the most widely used 95-octane Eurosuper increase by 5.7 percent to stand at SIT 162.60 (0.78 euro), comes about due to the rising U.S. dollar. ZAGREB - The new leadership of the Croatian and Slovene national electrical distributors HEP and ELES met, with the aim to re-establish the traditionally good relations which have been suspended by the unresolved status of the Krsko Nuclear Plant (NEK). 

 FRIDAY, 3 November LJUBLJANA - Bank of Slovenia intervenes on foreign exchange for the third time in a week. 

 BANK OF SLOVENIA Central Bank Intervenes on Foreign Exchange Market Again The Bank of Slovenia once again changed the base exchange rate on Friday, which is the third intervention by the central bank on the foreign exchange market in a week. The new base exchange rate for the euro is SIT 210.51. The difference between the base rate and the highest selling rate or the lowest buying rate must not exceed 0.2 percent. All three interventions come in a bid to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate, which according to the bank is still too low. 

 TAXATION Tax Office Issues Orders on Income Tax Statements By the end of September the Slovene Tax Administration had received a total of 1,139,059 income tax statements for 1999. At the end of October the Administration had issued orders for 98.9 percent of these statements. According to the orders, 14.7 percent of tax payers will have to make supplementary payments, 67.22 percent will receive a return, while 18.08 percent will neither receive a return or have to make supplementary payments. The average supplementary payment stands at SIT 73,742, while the average return stands at SIT 36,263. 

 COMPANIES Brewery Carries Out Takeover Bid for Mineral Water Producer Radenska Slovene brewery Pivovarna Lasko had successfully concluded its takeover bid for mineral water producer Radenska after it gained 73.73 percent of Radenska's shares in the period from 18 September to 27 October. This had brought Pivovarna Lasko's total ownership stake in Radenska to 83.93 percent. Officials of both companies expressed belief that the takeover and the consequent joint appearance on the market will bring better results in addition to an greater market share. Pivovarna Lasko informed Radenska of its intent of purchasing the majority stake in the company on 6 September. At an extraordinary general meeting on 24 October, shareholders of Pivovarna Lasko took a decision on the exchange of Pivovarna Lasko's shares for that of Radenska at a ratio of 1 to 1.7. 

 STATISTICS October Inflation at 0.6 Percent Prices stabilized in October after having risen considerably in September. The monthly inflation rate in October amounted to 0.6 percent, which is still slightly up over October 1999. Consumer prices have risen by 7.6 percent since the beginning of the year and gained nine percent in a year-on-year comparison. 

 STOCK EXCHANGE Ljubljana Stock Exchange Sees Low Turnover The turnover at the Ljubljana Stock Exchange totaled SIT 1.5 billion (7.1 million) last week. The turnover with securities at the official market accounted for 43 percent of the overall turnover. The share index SBI 20 remained practically unchanged, closing the week at 1,680.89 points. The authorised investment companies' index PIX increased by 1.56 percent to stand at 1375.21 points, while the free market index increased by 0.05 percent to 1473.06 points. Most turnover at the free market was recorded with company shares (SIT 396 million/euro 1.8 million), followed by authorised investment companies' shares (SIT 296 million/euro 1.4 million), bonds (SIT 142 million/euro 676,000) and pension vouchers (SIT 17 million/euro 81,000).

title: News Roundup - Monday, 30 October.
text:
Ljubljana, 30 October (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Monday, 30 October: 

 LJUBLJANA - Slovenia is pleased with a heavy turnout at the Kosovo local elections, and is convinced that despite persistent problems the elections represent a step towards democratisation and stabilisation of the province. This was written in a Foreign Ministry press release. The ministry also expressed content over the facts that during the elections no major incidents occurred and that the elections were carried out in line with international democratic standards, the ministry said. Moreover, the ministry expects that such conditions will be created as soon as possible so as to enable all eligible voters to go to the polls. 

 PORTOROZ - A two-day OSCE seminar on trust and security building measures in the Mediterranean opened with an address by Foreign Minister Lojze Peterle, who attached the key importance in building trust and security among nations to what he called "the culture of transparency". OSCE Secretary General Jan Kubis and the President of OSCE Parliamentary Assembly Adrian Severin, who addressed the meeting as well, stressed the need to consolidate the ties among the countries members of the Organisation for Peace and Co-operation in Europe and Mediterranean countries. 

 LJUBLJANA - The LDS, a party with 34 seats in parliament, resumed informal talks on the formation of a new government coalition. Talks are being held today with the Pensioners' Party, which has four seats, the Party of the Slovene Youth, also four seats, and the United List of Social Democrats, which has eleven seats in parliament. The DeSUS revleaed that "the contents of informal talks with the LDS on the formation of a new government coalition have been conducted so as to expect that the DeSUS might enter a coalition," its President Janko Kusar said. 

 LJUBLJANA - On the eve of the Reformation Day, a central ceremony will be held in the Slovene capital later in the evening. Slovenia, a country whose population is mainly Catholic, remembers the Protestant Reformation movement inspired by Luther and embodied in Slovenia in Protestant priest Primoz Trubar (1508-1586). It was Trubar who published the first Slovene book 450 years ago. According to Senior of the Evangelical Church in Slovenia Geza Ernisa, the Reformation Day is an occasion to regard the holiday not merely as a church holiday, but a holiday of all Slovenes. "It is right for Slovenia to pay a lot of attention to the holiday not only to mark Trubar's memory but to reevaluate the impact of his work on the present situation," said Ernisa. 

 LJUBLJANA - Only a fortnight after this year's parliamentary elections Delo published a monthly opinion poll in which the LDS won the support of 38.6 percent of those questioned, which is over two percent more than in the 15 october elections and considerably more than in the survey a month ago, when the LDS enjoyed the support of 19 percent of those questioned. According to the daily's commentator, the situation is different in the case of other parliamentary parties as these got much lower support in the survey than they did in the elections, while all improved their rating compared to the survey published by Delo a month ago. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Bank of Slovenia intervened again on the foreign exchange market in a bid to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank believes that the current growth of the exchange rate is still too low. The base exchange rate was fixed today at SIT 210.40 (on Friday it was set at SIT 210.25) for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. The measure takes effect on 2 November. The base exchange rate and the maximum difference serve as the basis to calculate the lowest purchase price and the highest selling price at which foreign currencies are sold by banks bound by contract with the central bank. These banks will buy foreign exchange at the lowest price of SIT 209.9792 (SIT 209.8295 set on Friday) for one euro. The rates apply to the market on which foreign exchange is purchased and sold by companies 

 BRUSSELS - Two Slovene environmental projects will be partly funded from the ISPA, the fund through which the EU helps ten Central European EU candidate countries in the fields of transport and environment. This was approved today by the fund. Slovenia will use the funds for a new purifying plant for waste waters in the city of Celje, 100 kilometres northeast of Ljubljana, and for modernisation of the sewage system in Lendava, northeastern Slovenia. The ISPA fund will allocate 8.84 million euros for the cleaning device worth 14.74 million euros, and 5.12 million euros for the other project in the value of 11.56 million euros. Together with the Phare and SAPARD programmes, the ISPA is one of the main three instruments of financial aid provided by the EU to Central European candidate countries for EU membership. 

 LJUBLJANA - Slovenia's Trade and Investment Office was presented 15,000 D-marks' worth technical equipment by a representative of the German Embassy, Michael Herrmann. A laptop and a projector were donated by the German government under a bilateral advisory programme called Transform and will be used for Slovenia's promotion abroad, said Office Director Matej Kovac, who accepted the gift. 

 LJUBLJANA - Prices stabilized in October after having risen considerably in September. The monthly inflation rate in October amounted to 0.6 percent, which is still slightly up over October 1999. Consumer prices have risen by 7.6 percent since the beginning of the year and gained nine percent in a year-on-year comparison, the National Statistical Office said. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Slovene share index, SBI 20, has dropped 0.26 percent since Friday to stand at 1676.40 points at today's close on the Ljubljana Stock Exchange. 

 LIMA - Slovenia's Miro Kregar has won the triathlon of Inkaman on Lake Titicaca, the world's largest lake, which separates Peru from Bolivia, and thus repeated his success of 1998. title: BS  Intervenes  on the  Foreign Exchange  Market Again.
text:
Ljubljana, 30 October (STA) - The Bank of Slovenia (BS) intervened again on the foreign exchange market on Monday in a bid to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank believes that the current growth of the exchange rate is still too low. The base exchange rate was fixed at SIT 210.40 (on Friday it was set at SIT 210.25) for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. The measure takes effect on 2 November. 

 The base exchange rate and the maximum difference serve as the basis to calculate the lowest purchase price and the highest selling price at which foreign currencies are sold by banks bound by contract with the central bank. These banks will buy foreign exchange at the lowest price of SIT 209.9792 (SIT 209.8295 set on Friday) for one euro. The rates apply to the market on which foreign exchange is purchased and sold by companies. 

 In exchange offices the exchange rate for the Deutsche mark calculated in euros can be up to 0.2 percent higher than the highest selling price or lower than the lowest purchase price. In the case of the currencies of the other members of the European Economic and Monetary Union, Switzerland, the U.K. and the U.S. the maximum difference is 0.4 percent. 

 The Bank of Slovenia will change the base exchange rate according to trends on the foreign exchange market and the domestic money market and in agreement with the objectives of its monetary policy. The exchange rate change has to be respected by all 22 commercial banks that signed a contract on co-operation in foreign exchange market interventions in March 2000. title: Weekly Review of the Slovene Economy from 21 to 27 October.

Ljubljana, 29 October (STA) - Slovene bank Abanka sold shares of another Slovene bank, SKB, last Tuesday. Austrian bank Raiffeisen Zentralbank however told Austrian business daily, Wirtschaftsblatt, that it had bought 11 percent of SKB shares for its clients on the Ljubljana Stock Exchange at the beginning of the week. On Thursday, Chairman of the SKB board, Cvetka Selsek, told Slovene daily Delo that SKB had been informed by Nova Ljubljanska banka (NLB) about Raiffeisen having 6.45 percent of SKB shares on a NLB fiduciary account. SKB is Slovenia's third largest bank in terms of its total assets, holding an over 11-percent market share. 

 CHRONOLOGY SATURDAY, 21 October 

 LJUBLJANA - Prices of liquefied gas and natural gas went up 5.42 percent and 9 percent, respectively. 

 MONDAY, 23 October 

 LJUBLJANA - The 10th information technology show Infos 2000 began, featuring 139 exhibitors. Winding up on Friday, the show mainly focussed on e-commerce, information technology in public administration, knowledge for development, challenges of e-technology and information infrastructure. 

 TUESDAY, 24 October 

 LJUBLJANA - The management of the Pension and Disability Insurance Institute (ZPIZ) discussed the financial situation of the institute, establishing that in order to pay out pensions by the end of this year a loan of SIT 31 billion (euro 148.3 million) will have to be taken out. 

 LJUBLJANA - President of the European Court of Auditors Jan Karlsson concluded a two-day visit. On Monday he met with a delegation from the Slovene Court of Auditors to discuss Slovenia's preparations to enter the EU, and with the leadership of the Slovene Chamber of Commerce (GZS), who introduced him to the Slovene macro-economic policy and GZS's role in it. 

 LJUBLJANA - The 7th international biannual fair Medilab opened, through Friday. Medilab is one of the most important professional shows in Slovenia, reflecting the development of Slovene and international laboratory technology, pharmaceutics, rehabilitation equipment and services. The show featured 368 exhibitors from 21 countries. 

 WEDNESDAY, 25 October 

 LJUBLJANA - Speaker of the Parliament Janez Podobnik presented to Minister of Transport and Communications Anton Bergauer an ISO 9002 certificate for quality. The Ministry of Transport and Communications and is the only Slovene ministry to have received the quality certificate. 

 THURSDAY, 26 October 

 BLED - Management College of Bled hosted a first European conference on knowledge management, which had been organized by Hanley Management College of Great Britain. The conference was an opportunity for participants from Europe and elsewhere to meet and exchange their views and experiences in management, development and improvements in information systems and technologies. 

 VELENJE - A 3rd two-day conference on human resource management began, organised by the Slovene business weekly, Gospodarski vestnik. 

 LJUBLJANA - The government decided that the Slovene Development Corporation (SRD) will supply Paloma with fresh capital by changing this manufacturer of paper-based products for personal hygiene's debts into a share in the company. 

 LJUBLJANA - The government also decided to supply fresh capital to the Fund for Regional Development Encouragement, the Slovene Export Corporation and the Fund for Small Business Development. 

 FRIDAY, 27 October 

 LJUBLJANA - A Bled-based hotel was sold to a rubber manufacturer. A contract to sell Grand hotel Toplice Bled to Sava Kranj was signed with the Slovene Compensation Corporation, which brought lengthy efforts to denationalise and privatise the hotel to an end. By purchasing the company, Sava prevented it from going bankrupt. 

 BANK OF SLOVENIA Central Bank Intervenes on Foreign Currency Market 

 The Bank of Slovenia intervened on the foreign exchange market on Friday to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank believed that the current growth of the exchange rate was too low. The base exchange rate had thus been fixed at SIT 210.25 for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. The base exchange rate and the maximum difference serve as the basis to calculate the lowest purchase price and the highest selling price at which foreign currencies are sold by banks bound by contract with the central bank. These banks will buy foreign exchange at the lowest price of SIT 209.8295 for one euro and sell foreign currencies at up to SIT 210.6705 for one euro as of 27 October. The rates apply to the market on which foreign exchange is purchased and sold by companies. 

 BANKS Gorenjska Banka's Total Assets up 18 Percent 

 Gorenjska banka made a gross profit of SIT 1.4 billion (6.69 million euros) in the first nine months of this year, which puts its return on capital at 8.9 percent. At the end of September the bank's total assets amounted to SIT 153.3 billion (733.4 million euros), up 18 percent from the end of 1999, when the bank placed 7th biggest bank on the Slovene market. 

 NLB Takes out Syndicated Loan of 140 Million Euros 

 Slovenia's largest commercial bank, Nova Ljubljanska banka (NLB), and a consortium of 27 foreign banks signed a contract on a mid-term syndicated loan of 140 million euros. This is the seventh syndicated loan taken out by NLB on the foreign money market. The bank will use about 30 percent of the funds to pay off the past loans, and the rest to finance export-oriented Slovene companies. The loan has to be paid off within five years at a variable interest rate called Euribor. 

 SKB Takes out Syndicated Loan of 50 Million Euros 

 Slovene bank SKB and a consortium of 13 foreign banks signed a contract on a long-term syndicated loan of 50 million euros. This is the seventh syndicated loan taken out by SKB on the foreign money market since 1994. The funds will be used to finance export-oriented Slovene companies. The loan was taken out at a raised variable interest rate Euribor of 0.40 percentage point. The bank did not wish to disclose other details about the loan. 

 INSURANCE MARKET Contract Signed Between Slovene First Pension Fund and Dutch Bank 

 A contract on long-term co-operation was signed between Slovenia's First Pension Fund and the Dutch ABN AMRO Bank which allows the bank to purchase more than nine percent of First Pension Fund's shares. The partnership between the two companies will enable First Pension Fund to enter the international financial market; by using the Dutch bank's infrastructure, the Slovene company will reduce operating costs and improve the safety of investment, thus increasing long-term return of capital. Amsterdam-based ABN Amro Bank as a financial institution ranks 16th in the world and fifth in Europe, employing 110,000 persons in 76 branch offices world-wide. 

 COMPANIES Shareholders of Pivovarna Lasko Opt for Increase in Share Capital 

 Shareholders of one of Slovenia's two major breweries took a decision at an extraordinary meeting to raise the company's share capital by issuing fresh shares in the nominal value of SIT 2.2 billion (10.5 million euros). 

 Microsoft Slovenia Records Fall in PC Sales 

 The sales of Microsoft Slovenia products totaled US$ 13.4 million in the period from July 1999 to June 2000. The number of PCs sold in this period dropped from 84,000 in the same period a year earlier to 80,000. A fall in PC sales was recorded for the first time by Microsoft Slovenia. However, larger clients with which long-term enterprise agreements are signed went up. 

 POWER INDUSTRY Use of Electricity Up 

 A total of 7.8 billion of Kilowatt hours of electricity was used in Slovenia in the first nine months of this year, up 4.4 percent from the same period last year and 4.6 percent above the plan. 

 STATISTICS Foreign Exchange Reserves Reach US$ 3.9 Billion at the End of August 

 Slovenia's foreign exchange reserves totalled US$ 3.998 billion at the end of August. Foreign reserves thus decreased by US$ 115 million from a month before, which is still lower than the overall foreign debt by US$ 1.786 billion, which totaled US$ 5.784 billion on the last day of August, according to the latest issue of the Bulletin of the Bank of Slovenia. The bulk of foreign exchange reserves, US$ 2.893 billion, were the reserves of the central bank, while the rest belonged to commercial banks. Foreign exchange reserves of the central bank dropped by US$ 165 million, while those of commercial banks increased by US$ 48 million over the end of 1999. 

 Foreign Debt at US$ 5.8 Billion 

 Slovenia's long-term foreign debt totaled US$ 5.687 billion and short-term debt US$ 97 million. Of the long-term debt US$ 2.73 billion was public and state-guaranteed debt and the rest of US$ 2.957 billion was private debt. Slovenia's foreign debt increased by US$ 293 million over the end of 1999. Long-term debt was up by US$ 313 million and short-term debt down by US$ 20 million. 

 Industrial Output up 3.7 Percent in September 

 September saw a 22.1-percent increase in industrial output from August, with a yearly increase standing at 3.7 percent, preliminary data released by the National Statistical Office show. Industrial output was up 7.7 percent in the January-to-September period in comparison with the same period last year. 

 Slovenia Visited by Over 1.5 Million Tourists in from January to September 

 In September, however, Slovene tourist resorts were visited by 190,353 tourists, up 12 percent from September 1999. The number of foreign tourists totalled 121,213, a rise of 24 percent from a year earlier. 

 STOCK EXCHANGE High Turnover on Ljubljana Stock Exchange 

 The Slovene Share Index, SBI 20, gained 1.55 percent during last week and finished at 1680.79 points. The authorised investment companies' index, PIX, followed the upward trend as it posted a gain of 2.69 percent and finished the week at 1354.03. The free market index, IPT, fell sharply on the other hand, losing 2.45 percent during the week to stand at 1472.19. Stock-brokers reported a total of 6,683 deals during the week, totaling some 33.65 million euros, which is more than twice the turnover seen a week before. A total of 32 package deals amounted for some SIT 5.1 billion or 72 percent of the week's total turnover. 

 EXCHANGE RATES Foreign Currencies Up 

 The euro edged up SIT 0.17 to SIT 209.30 last week. The Swiss franc lost SIT 0.14 to SIT 138.46, the US dollar gained SIT 4.11 to SIT 251.36 tolarja, the D-mark increased by SIT 0.10 to SIT 107.02, the Austrian schilling by SIT 0.02 to SIT 15.21, and 100 Italian lira by SIT 0.01 to SIT 10.81. title: News Roundup - Thursday, 26 October.
text:
Ljubljana, 26 October (STA) - Below is a roundup of major events on Thursdaqy, 26 October: 

 BUCHAREST - Slovenia expects from the new authorities of Yugoslavia, a country which was admitted to the club of countries taking part in the Balkan Stability Pact on Thursday, to fulfil their promises and to respect international law as well as procedures applicable to membership of international organisations. Furthermore, the FRY is expected to resume talks on succession issues regarding the former Yugoslavia in which all successor states are in an equal position, STA was told by the deputy national coordinator for the Stability Pact, Jozica Puhar, the head of the Slovene delegation at a two-day Bucharest gathering focussing on human rights and democratisation. 

 LJUBLJANA - The government approved aid to the people of Yugoslavia at its session. The proposal to send medicines, food and school requisites worth nearly DEM 47,000 to Yugoslavia was put forward by the Foreign Ministry and Slovenia's Red Cross. By sending the relief Slovenia wants to contribute to alleviating difficult conditions in Yugoslavia and consolidating democratic changes in the country, the Foreign Ministry said. 

 LJUBLJANA - Despite an agreement between the Slovene and Croatian police the number of illegal immigrants coming to Slovenia from Croatia has not fallen, Director General of the Slovene Police Marko Pogorevc wrote in a letter to the Croatian Deputy Interior Minister. The Slovene police has apprehended this week large groups of illegal immigrants along the border with Croatia. As soon as they were apprehended, the immigrants asked for asylum in Slovenia. Only on Wednesday more than 200 illegal immigrants were apprehended. Pogorevc also expressed hope that Croatian policemen will more active in preventing illegal migrations be in the future. 

 BUENOS AIRES - Two Slovene tourists were shot dead in an armed robbery in Bolivia on Tuesday, while one was injured and is being treated in hospital in the Bolivian capital, the Slovene Foreign Ministry confirmed for STA. Three Slovene tourists were riding horses in the wilds of Bolivia when they were joined by two men. They were all riding together for several hours when the two men surrounded the Slovene tourists and opened fire. One of the Slovene citizens pretended to be dead and was later found by local people who took him to hospital. His fellows were shot dead. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Slovene Diplomats' Trade Union criticized the personnel policy of the Foreign Ministry, stating in a press release that diplomacy should be professional in order to be able to successfully represent the interests of the country. Diplomats should be highly skilled and creative experts, the trade union wrote, adding that diplomatic posts should not be rewards for past work or even a place "to deposit redundant members of political parties". 

 THE VATICAN - A mass was celebrated before 4,000 pilgrims who took part in a Slovene pilgrimage to Rome in the Holy Year 2000. After the mass, which was offered in St. Peter's Basilica by Ljubljana Archbishop and Slovene Metropolitan Franc Rode, pilgrims were joined by the Pope John Paul II, who addressed them in Slovene. Slovene Catholics' pilgrimage to Rome in the Holy Year 2000 began on Tuesday, it is attended by eight Slovene bishops and will wind up tomorrow. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Bank of Slovenia will intervene on the foreign exchange market tomorrow to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank believes that the current growth of the exchange rate is too low. The base exchange rate has been fixed at SIT 210.25 for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. The base exchange rate and the maximum difference serve as the basis to calculate the lowest purchase price and the highest selling price at which foreign currencies are sold by banks bound by contract with the central bank. These banks will buy foreign exchange at the lowest price of SIT 209.8295 for one euro and sell foreign currencies at up to SIT 210.6705 for one euro as of 27 October. The rates apply to the market on which foreign exchange is purchased and sold by companies. 

 PIRAN - Competitive pressure will increase considerably in Central and Eastern European countries once they have become EU member countries. Moreover, the social element of economy will no longer be present, for which reason EU candidate countries should put social policy before integration into the EU, with trade unions having to play a central role in accession, said Wolfgang Weinz, coordinator for Central and Eastern Europe, IUF, International Union of Food, Agriculture, Hotel, Restaurant, Catering, Tobacco and Allied Workers' Associations, at the beginning of a two-day meeting of the Slovene trade unions of agriculture and food industry, and of tourism which began on the Slovene coast. 

 LJUBLJANA - The Slovene share index, SBI 20, edged up 0.69 percent to stand at 1681.52 points at today's close. 

 SYDNEY - Athlete Dragica Lapornik won a bronze medal in shot put, securing Slovenia a third medal at the 2000 Paraolympics. 

 SARAJEVO - Two actors from a Ljubljana-based theatre ensemble received the Gold Laurel Wreath for best actress and best actor in Moliere's Misanthrope, a Slobodan Unkovski-directed production which was shown at the Sarajevo festival of experimental theatre, MESS 2000, last Sunday. Polona Juh and Jernej Sugman from the Slovene National Theatre (SNG) were awarded on Thursday evening in Sarajevo. 

 LJUBLJANA - A retrospective of one of Slovenia's finest minimalist artists opened at the Museum of Modern Art featuring 100 paintings and drawings from the past 30 years. Gustav Gnamus, a full professor at the Ljubljana Academy of Fine Arts since 1990, is a recipient of the 1992 Preseren Fund Prize and the 1996 Jakopic Award for outstanding achievement in fine arts. The artist, born in 1941, studied at the Ljubljana Academy of Fine Arts with several most distinguished Slovene modernist, including Gabrijel Stupica (1913-1990). After his first solo exhibition in 1969, Gnamus has exhibited a lot as part of group exhibitions at home and abroad. 

 KRANJ - Uros Zupan, one of the most promising Slovene poets, is the recipient of the 2000 Jenko Award, a prize awarded by the Slovene Writers' Association for best collection of poems from the past two years. The prize-winning ceremony will take place tonight at the Preseren Theatre in the city of Kranj, 25 kilometres north of Ljubljana. Zupan, a lyric poet par excellence who was awarded for his collection of poems entitled "A Tree and a Sparrow", a kind of a cut through ten years of his career, was chosen by a five-member jury. 

 LJUBLJANA - A Slovene mountaineer has died attempting to climb Dorje Lakpa in the Himalayas. Andrej Zaman died just below the mountain peak, the Slovene Mountaineers' Association said, but had no further information as yet available. (konec)sk/eho STA027 2000-10-26/18:59.

title: Central Bank  to  Intervene  on the  Foreign Exchange  Market.
text:
Ljubljana, 26 October (STA) - The Bank of Slovenia will intervene on the foreign exchange market on Friday to influence the growth of the foreign exchange rate. The central bank believes that the current growth of the exchange rate is too low. The base exchange rate has been fixed at SIT 210.25 for one euro with the maximum difference of 0.2 percent. 

 The base exchange rate and the maximum difference serve as the basis to calculate the lowest purchase price and the highest selling price at which foreign currencies are sold by banks bound by contract with the central bank. These banks will buy foreign exchange at the lowest price of SIT 209.8295 for one euro and sell foreign currencies at up to SIT 210.6705 for one euro as of 27 October. The rates apply to the market on which foreign exchange is purchased and sold by companies. 

 In exchange offices the exchange rate for the Deutsche mark calculated in euros can be up to 0.2 percent higher than the highest selling price or lower than the lowest purchase price. In the case of the currencies of the other members of the European Economic and Monetary Union, Switzerland, the U.K. and the U.S. the maximum difference is 0.4 percent. 

 The Bank of Slovenia will change the base exchange rate according to trends on the foreign exchange market and the domestic money market and in agreement with the objectives of its monetary policy. The exchange rate change has to be respected by all 22 commercial banks that signed a contract on co-operation in foreign exchange market interventions in March 2000.
